Snapline 2.12.0

Screen recordings can carry sound: your microphone, what your Mac is playing, or both — each its own track in the movie.

New

  • Microphone and System Audio for recordings. Two toggles, in Settings → General and right on the Record Screen bar. Each source is written as its own track, never mixed, so an editor can pull either apart later. Both are off by default — a recording stays silent until you say otherwise.
  • Pick your microphone. The Record Screen bar lists every connected input. Your choice sticks; if the device isn't connected at record time, Snapline says so, records with the system default, and shows the missing device as "not connected" until you re-pick.

Notes

  • A recording never fails because of the microphone. Access refused, no input device, or a microphone unplugged mid-take — Snapline tells you at the time, and the video (and any system audio) is exactly what it would have been.
  • Audio stays in step with the picture through pauses, stalls, and long takes — gaps are healed rather than letting the soundtrack drift.
  • Snapline's own notification pills no longer appear in recordings.
  • Recorded audio stays inside the movie file on your Mac; nothing is uploaded. Snapline asks for microphone access only when you turn Microphone on — the privacy policy spells it out.

Snapline 2.11.0

Capture Set now shoots the whole set in one go, and the editor stops stacking windows.

Capture Set

  • One arm, many shots. Arming a Capture Set opens the region crosshair right away, and each shot you take reopens it for the next panel — no hotkey press between captures. Press Esc to pause the chain; the pill's Capture button or the region hotkey picks it back up. Done still combines the set.
  • See the set as you build it. The pill shows the captures themselves as a strip, in slot order, instead of a bare count — and shots that join the set no longer raise a Quick Access card each.

Fixes

  • Opening a capture that is already in the editor — a thumbnail clicked again, or Edit from its pinned window — now brings that editor to front instead of opening a second one.
  • The Capture Set pill keeps its count line centered once the hint hides.
  • License hardening: a bare copied key file can no longer share one seat across several online Macs. Existing activations are untouched.

Try everything free for 14 days

Snapline now starts as a full-featured trial: every capture mode, recording, and editor feature works for 14 days, with no card, no account, and no sign-up. When the trial ends, capture locks until a license is entered — History, the editor, and text recognition stay open, because those hold captures you already made.

  • Already tried Snapline before the trial existed? If this install was unlicensed, a fresh 14 days starts the first time you launch this version — deliberately, so you can judge the whole app rather than a paywall.
  • Quiet by design: no banners, no nags. In the final days, a small "N days left · Buy Snapline" countdown appears in the status menu and the License pane, and that's all.
  • Trials are dated by Snapline's server, so a reinstall doesn't restart one.

Activation goes online — and runs offline

Pasting your license key now makes one quick check that claims this Mac's seat. After that, everything works offline: launches, captures, and every feature verify locally, with no account and no sign-in.

  • One seat, one Mac: a license activates on as many Macs at once as its seat count. Moving is instant — deactivate in Settings → License on the old Mac, activate on the new one.
  • Already activated? Nothing to do. Your install keeps working untouched and upgrades itself silently the first time it's online.
  • The activation call carries your key and a salted hash of this Mac's hardware identifier — never the identifier itself. The privacy policy spells out exactly what's sent and stored.
